strengths: Provides a clean EOT/KL-regularized derivation showing standard attention as the uniform-prior special case and additive log-prior generalization; the math is simple and correct.

GOAT parameterizes the relative prior via Fourier features and a key-only sink bias, embedding both into Q/K vectors with a scaling trick so the mechanism remains compatible with standard SDPA/FlashAttention without dense L×L bias matrices.

The attention-sink analysis (collapse-to-prior theorem and context-sensitivity bounds) gives a useful first-principles explanation of a known empirical phenomenon, and the key-only sink parameterization is a reasonable way to decouple structural defaults from content representations.
The paper attempts breadth across language modeling, long-context retrieval, DNA, and vision, with claimed length extrapolation and memory savings that would be valuable if fully substantiated.

Appendix F makes an interesting attempt to justify the parameterization via SDPA-compatibility, translation equivariance, and boundedness, yielding a classification of admissible finite trigonometric relative priors.
weaknesses: The central generalization is close to trivial: an additive log-prior in the softmax is algebraically isomorphic to an additive positional encoding, as the authors themselves acknowledge in Appendix E. The advance over existing relative position biases, ALiBi, and T5-style learned biases is incremental and not isolated.

Experimental evidence is thin and largely qualitative: the main C4 result is a single 125M-parameter run with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; key figures (passkey, NIAH, ImageNet extrapolation, DNA NLL) are low-resolution and often lack exact numbers, so the claims of “outperforms” and “near-perfect” are not fully substantiated.

Critical ablations are missing: there is no controlled comparison against standard attention augmented with a learned additive relative bias or key-only sink bias, and no ablation over spectral rank R, prior initialization, sink MLP, dimension split d_c/d_p, or scaling choices. It is therefore unclear whether gains come from the EOT prior formulation or simply from extra structured capacity/tuned biases.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or implementation details are provided for Fourier frequencies, sink MLP, 2D factorization, synthetic copy-mixture task, baseline training, or hardware. Appendix G/H gives some hyperparameters but omits seeds, hyperparameter search, and preprocessing, and the claimed 36% memory reduction is unexplained.

Several theoretical claims are overstated. The “unique” restriction to finite trigonometric priors depends on strong assumptions such as boundedness and finite SDPA dimension that are not necessary for stable attention. The max-entropy recency justification fixes an arbitrary mean-lag constraint, and the sink theorem assumes a uniform margin and low-signal limit.

Baselines are limited mainly to RoPE, ALiBi, and sinusoidal absolute PE, with no comparisons to T5 relative bias, Kerple, FIRE, xPos, or 2D position methods. The vision experiment uses only a learnable absolute-PE baseline, weakening the generality claim across modalities.

Presentation and editing are poor: inconsistent notation (Goat/GOAT), broken appendix formatting (“roof”, “###”), missing axis labels/colorbars in several figures, and incomplete or inconsistent references. The paper also lacks a limitations section and meaningful discussion of failure modes, compute costs, or dataset ethics.

strengths: The EOT/KL-prior framing yields a clean closed-form solution (softmax(s/τ + log π)) that unifies additive attention biases under a single derivation, and the presentation of this identity is pedagogically clear.

The SDPA-compatible implementation (block-diagonal content/positional subspaces plus pre-scaling by √d_h) is elegant: it absorbs the log-prior into a single unmodified FlashAttention call without materializing L×L bias matrices, and the deliberate choice to leave the prior unscaled by 1/√d_h is well-motivated.

The theoretical treatment of attention sinks (Theorem 5.1 'collapse to prior', Theorem 5.4 sensitivity bounds) is a reasonable formalization, and the explicit key-only bias u(j) is a sensible way to disentangle structural defaults from content representations.

The spectral (truncated Fourier) parameterization with signed coefficients is a legitimate way to allow repulsion patterns that positive-definite kernel approximations cannot express, and the toy copy-mixture experiment (Figure 1) provides some evidence that the sink and relative components are disentangled.
The paper is generally well-written and the figures are illustrative of the intended inductive biases.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result (Proposition 3.1) is essentially the textbook fact that KL-regularized transport yields softmax(s + log π), which is algebraically identical to adding an additive bias to attention logits. The paper itself acknowledges this isomorphism in Appendix E, so the 'missing term'/'generalization' framing largely re-labels existing additive-bias methods (ALiBi, T5 relative bias, etc.) rather than providing new mathematical content.

The Appendix F 'optimality' results are conditional on self-imposed constraints (SDPA-compatibility, translation equivariance, boundedness). They do not uniquely derive the parameterization from data or first principles, yet the introduction claims they 'prove ... uniquely restricts the admissible priors to a finite trigonometric family.' This overstates the force of the result and the constraint choices are not independently justified.

Empirical validation is too thin to support the paper's strong claims. The language-modeling result rests on a single 125M model, a single dataset (C4), and a single training run; the headline '1.55 points over ALiBi' is a single number in an inset. Most figures (Figures 3–5) have no error bars or seed variation.

Baselines are limited to RoPE, ALiBi, sinusoidal, and position-interpolated RoPE. There is no comparison to other additive/relative-bias mechanisms (e.g., T5 relative bias, FIRE, Kerple, Sandwich) or to other sink-handling approaches (e.g., register/'no-op' tokens), despite the paper claiming the prior framing is a general improvement over existing encodings.

No ablation studies are provided for the method's multiple design choices (spectral prior vs. sink bias vs. uniform initialization vs. the ALiBi-style recency init), so it is impossible to attribute the reported gains to any specific component.

The biological-sequence experiment reports N=3 continuations and noisy correlation metrics (r=0.466 vs 0.320), which is far too little evidence for a claimed improvement; the vision experiment uses only ViT-Small and shows modest accuracy differences without uncertainty estimates.
The claimed 36% peak-memory reduction (2.86→1.83 GB) versus RoPE is not mechanistically explained and may be confounded by implementation details rather than a property of the mechanism.

The paper has no limitations section and the impact statement is generic; potential failure modes (e.g., cases where a learned prior hurts, sensitivity to frequency initialization, extra head-dimension overhead from d_p) are not discussed.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code release or seeds are mentioned, the exact GOAT configuration (number of frequencies R, initialization of α/β, sink MLP details) is only partially specified, and baseline hyperparameters are not given.

strengths: The EOT/KL-prior reframing is elegant and yields a clean, closed-form generalization of attention (softmax(s/τ + log π)), which provides a principled lens for interpreting positional biases and attention sinks. The derivation in Section 3 and Appendix A is correct and easy to follow.

The parameterization trick (Eqs. 20-21, Algorithm 1) that absorbs the additive log-prior into a single unmodified SDPA call via composite query/key vectors is genuinely clever and practically valuable: it preserves head dimension, avoids materializing L×L bias matrices, and remains FlashAttention-compatible. This is a real engineering advantage over many additive-bias alternatives.

Appendix F is the strongest theoretical contribution: Theorem 2 (classification of SDPA-compatible, translation-equivariant, bounded relative priors as finite trigonometric polynomials), the max-entropy justification of the ALiBi-style recency term (Theorem 3, Prop F.6), and the rank-one characterization of key-only sinks (Theorem 4) are rigorous and non-trivial.

The analysis of attention sinks (Theorem 5.1 collapse-to-prior, Theorem 5.4 context-sensitivity bounds) gives a first-principles account of a widely observed phenomenon, and connects the peaked-prior margin δ to a logarithmic stability requirement (δ ~ ln L), which is a useful and interpretable result.

The experimental breadth is a plus: language modeling on C4 with length extrapolation and NIAH/passkey retrieval, DNA modeling, and ViT resolution extrapolation show the mechanism is not confined to 1D sequences.
The paper is generally well written and the synthetic copy-mixture ablation (Figure 1) nicely validates that the relative and sink components are learned as disentangled, interpretable structure.
weaknesses: The central derivation (Prop 3.1) is essentially standard KL-regularized softmax and is well known in the EOT/RL literature; the paper's novelty lies mostly in the parameterization and the sink analysis, so the framing overstates the depth of the core theoretical step.

The claim that standard PEs are 'heuristic approximations' of an EOT-'mandated' prior is over-claimed. Appendix E itself concedes that priors and positional encodings are algebraically isomorphic and that GOAT is 'operationally a positional encoding.' The real contribution is a disentangled additive parameterization, not a derivation that 'mandates' a form, and the main text should be framed accordingly.

Experimental evidence is thinner than the claims suggest. The DNA results rely on N=3 continuations (r=0.466 vs 0.320) and are described as 'improvements and parity,' which is weak. The ImageNet experiment compares only against absolute PE rather than the more relevant RoPE-based or 2D learned-PE ViTs, and the 'learned 2D shift-invariant prior' is shown only qualitatively (Figure 5b).
No error bars or multiple-seed runs are reported for the language-modeling, retrieval, or vision results, making it hard to assess whether reported gaps (e.g., 1.55 PPL over ALiBi) are robust.

The 36% peak-memory reduction (2.86 GB → 1.83 GB) in Figure 4b is a headline efficiency claim, but the mechanism is not explained in the main text. Since standard attention does not materialize bias matrices under FlashAttention, it is unclear why GOAT should reduce memory rather than merely being comparable; this needs clarification (e.g., reduced content dimension/KV cache).

Several conclusions rest on figures whose full experimental detail is deferred or absent (e.g., Passkey/NIAH training lengths, GOAT configuration for retrieval, number of runs), limiting reproducibility despite the appendix hyperparameter tables.

The 'optimality' language in Appendix F.5 is conditional on self-selected constraints (SDPA-compatibility, translation equivariance, boundedness); presenting it as optimality of the parameterization somewhat overstates what is proven, since alternative constraint sets could admit different families.

strengths: Provides an elegant and mathematically clean EOT-based generalization of attention: replacing the implicit uniform prior with an arbitrary prior π yields the closed-form solution softmax(s/τ + log π), framing standard attention as a special case and casting positional encodings as heuristic approximations of an EOT-derived prior.

Introduces a practical and efficient parameterization (GOAT) that realizes the log-prior as an additive term inside a single SDPA call. The spectral decomposition of relative position via Fourier features, the key-only sink bias, and the composite query/key construction allow compatibility with optimized kernels like FlashAttention without materializing dense L×L bias matrices.

Provides a formal treatment of attention sinks through the EOT lens: Theorem 5.1 (collapse to prior under low content signal) and Theorem 5.4 (context sensitivity bounds) formalize why a default attention pattern must exist and how a peaked prior can stabilize low-signal regimes. The explicit sink parameterization decouples structural defaults from content representations.

Offers broad empirical validation across modalities: synthetic copy-mixture, C4 125M language modeling, 1.23B FineWeb language modeling, passkey retrieval, needle-in-a-haystack, DNA sequence modeling, ImageNet resolution extrapolation, and spatial VQA. The length extrapolation results are particularly compelling (e.g., 1.23B GOAT reaches 24.77 PPL at 16k versus RoPE's 417.43).

Includes useful ablations and analysis: Fourier mode count, frequency grid, initialization, learned spectral structure, per-head amplitude, directional coefficients, and training loss checkpoints. These support the design choices and show that GOAT does not slow early optimization.

Reproducibility details are reasonably thorough for an architecture paper: appendices provide dataset names, model sizes, optimizer settings, schedules, batch sizes, precision, and GOAT-specific configurations for the main experiments.
weaknesses: The 1.23B-parameter language modeling comparison only includes RoPE as a baseline. ALiBi, a fixed additive positional encoding known for strong length extrapolation, is omitted at the billion-parameter scale despite being a natural and important baseline for the paper's central claim. While ALiBi appears in the 125M and NIAH/passkey experiments, the absence at 1.23B weakens the claim that GOAT combines the extrapolation robustness of fixed encodings with the flexibility of learned priors at scale.

The method fixes the total head dimension, so GOAT reduces the content subspace to d_c = d_h - d_p and scales content logits by 1/√d_c instead of the standard 1/√d_h. This changes both content capacity and effective temperature relative to the baselines. No ablation isolates the effect of the learned prior from these architectural and scaling confounds, making it unclear how much of the gain is due to the prior versus reduced content dimension or sharper content logits.

Long-context evaluation relies heavily on synthetic retrieval tasks (passkey, NIAH). There is no evaluation on standard real-world long-context benchmarks such as RULER, LongBench, or downstream long-document reasoning. Some additional experiments are small-scale or preliminary: the DNA results report N=3 continuations without error bars, and the spatial VQA gains (20.3% vs 17.2%) are modest and may be within noise.

Several claims are somewhat overstated. 'Standard attention is asymptotically unstable' in Theorem 5.4 is conditional on a uniform prior and no content sink; standard Transformers often learn content-based sinks, so the theorem compares priors rather than proving instability of standard attention as deployed. 'Avoiding representational trade-offs' is argued theoretically but not directly measured. The EOT explanation of sinks is essentially a formalization of collapse to the prior under a peaked prior, not a derivation of why standard models learn sinks in the first place.

The optimality discussion in Appendix G is conditional on deliberately chosen constraints (SDPA-compatibility, translation equivariance, boundedness). The classification theorem is mathematically sound but does not establish that GOAT's parameterization is universally optimal; the paper is careful in places but the framing can read as stronger than warranted.

Reproducibility is not fully adequate: no code release is mentioned, random seeds are not reported, and compute details (GPU type, training time, total FLOPs) are absent for the large-scale runs. The reported 36% peak-memory reduction in the DNA experiment is not explained, and no explicit limitations section is provided; the impact statement is generic.

There are minor presentation and technical issues: Equation 20 is missing a '+' between the cosine and sine terms; notation is occasionally inconsistent (e.g., K, K_rel, K_ij, u(j)); the vision and multimodal handling of the sink term u(j) is not fully specified; and the absolute-position component u(j) depends on j/L_train and log(1+j)/log(1+L_train), which may not extrapolate cleanly beyond the training window.

strengths: Provides a clean EOT/KL-regularized derivation showing that replacing Shannon entropy with KL to a prior yields softmax(s/τ + log π); this formally links additive log-priors to attention and gives a unified view of standard attention as the uniform-prior case.

The GOAT implementation is elegant: it factorizes query/key vectors into content and positional subspaces and uses a scaling trick so the additive log-prior is realized inside a single unmodified SDPA/FlashAttention call without materializing L×L bias matrices.

Empirical scope is broad: 125M C4 language modeling, 1.23B FineWeb scaling, passkey/NIAH retrieval, DNA modeling, ImageNet resolution extrapolation, and spatial VQA; the 1.23B FineWeb table shows a dramatic extrapolation gap (e.g., 16k context: RoPE 417.43 vs GOAT 24.77) and the 125M C4 results improve over ALiBi.

The appendices contain detailed derivations, including a proof that finite-dimensional SDPA-compatible translation-equivariant bounded relative priors are finite trigonometric polynomials, and a max-entropy justification for an ALiBi-like recency term.
The attention-sink analysis provides an intuitive formal account of sinks as prior collapse in low-signal regimes, and the explicit key-only sink bias is a sensible disentangled parameterization.
Ablations on Fourier modes, frequency grid, and initialization are included, and training hyperparameters are reported in appendices.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited: KL-regularized attention with an arbitrary prior is a standard convex optimization result, and the practical GOAT parameterization is essentially a learned additive relative position bias with Fourier features plus a key-only bias. Prior work on additive relative biases (T5, Shaw et al.) and Fourier features for relative position (e.g., FLT, FIRE) already covers much of the mechanism; Appendix F even concedes that GOAT is operationally a positional encoding, so the claimed conceptual distinction between “prior” and “PE” is largely semantic.

Several theoretical claims are overstated or trivial. Proposition 3.1 is a one-line softmax reparameterization; Theorem 5.1 (collapse to prior) is a simple bound on a bounded-logit softmax; Theorem 5.4’s sensitivity bound follows directly from the definition and does not establish that standard attention is practically unstable. Appendix G proves optimality only within constraints chosen to fit the authors’ parameterization and explicitly excludes the unbounded recency/sink terms that GOAT actually uses.

Missing baselines weaken the empirical claims. Language modeling does not compare against learned additive relative position biases (T5 buckets, Shaw et al., FIRE) or strong long-context RoPE variants (position interpolation, NTK, YaRN) in the main scaling table; ImageNet compares only to absolute PE; DNA compares only to RoPE. The 1.23B table has no ALiBi baseline.

The comparisons are confounded by capacity changes. GOAT reserves d_p = 2R + 2 dimensions for the prior and reduces the content subspace to d_c = d_h − d_p, while standard attention/RoPE use full d_h for content. No ablation matches content dimension or shows that gains come from the prior rather than from this architectural trade-off and the modified content scaling.

The efficiency claim is unsupported. GOAT uses the same head dimension and same SDPA kernel, yet reports a 36% peak-memory reduction versus RoPE on DNA; no mechanism explains how this happens, and it likely reflects a different baseline implementation rather than a benefit of GOAT. The claim of “no computational overhead” ignores the extra positional features/MLP computation and the reduced content capacity.

Length-extrapolation evidence is confounded by the absolute-position MLP in u(j). The paper trains that MLP on L_train and does not show u(j) beyond the training length, nor does it ablate the MLP versus a purely relative/recency parameterization. Thus the claim of combining learned positional embeddings with fixed-encoding extrapolation is not isolated.

The sink experiments do not directly test the theoretical prediction against strong controls. Standard models also learn sinks via content norms, and no experiment measures context sensitivity or compares GOAT’s prior sink to a baseline with an additive sink bias (e.g., a learned key bias in standard attention).

Experimental rigor and reproducibility are weak: no error bars, no multiple seeds, no statistical tests, several results only in plots without exact numbers, and no code release. Some sections appear incomplete or truncated (e.g., the sentence in Section 5 ending “weak or am”).

Presentation is poor: inconsistent notation (GOAT/Goat), missing plus signs in Eq. (20), garbled equations in the text, repeated header “You Need Better Attention Priors,” and mislabeled references (e.g., Litman 2025 appears as 2022; Cuturi 2013 as 2023; Dai et al. 2019 as 2023).

Limitations and ethics discussion are inadequate: there is no limitations section, no discussion of failure modes, compute costs, negative results, or potential harms; the Impact Statement is generic and adds little.

The overall significance is not established. Because the method is an incremental combination of known components and the empirical gains are not cleanly attributed to the EOT-prior framework, it is unclear whether GOAT advances the field beyond existing additive relative-position and long-context methods.

strengths: Provides a clean and correct EOT/KL-regularized derivation of attention, showing standard softmax attention as the uniform-prior special case and generalizing it to softmax(s/τ + log π).

The GOAT parameterization is elegant and practical: relative Fourier features are factored into query/key dot products, and the key-only sink bias is implemented with one extra SDPA dimension, preserving FlashAttention compatibility without dense L×L bias matrices.

Empirical evidence is broad and often compelling: 125M C4 and 1.23B FineWeb experiments show strong length extrapolation over RoPE (e.g., 1.23B: RoPE 89.45/417.43 vs GOAT 22.69/24.77 at 8k/16k), plus passkey retrieval, NIAH, DNA, ImageNet resolution extrapolation, and spatial VQA results.

The attention-sink analysis (collapse to prior in low-signal regimes and sensitivity bounds) gives a useful theoretical lens for interpreting and controlling sinks as structural defaults rather than entangled content artifacts.
The appendix is thorough: proofs, ablations, hyperparameters, and implementation details support reproducibility and clarify the design choices.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the KL-prior generalization is a straightforward extension of existing EOT views, and Appendix F concedes that GOAT is algebraically an additive positional bias. Fourier relative features and key-only sink biases also overlap with prior work, so the main contribution is parameterization and framing rather than a fundamentally new attention mechanism.

The memory-efficiency claim is not well supported. GOAT should have essentially the same attention memory footprint as RoPE because the total head dimension is preserved, yet Figure 4(b) reports a 36% peak-memory reduction (2.86 GB to 1.83 GB) without explaining the baseline implementation or accounting for potential confounds.

Baseline coverage is incomplete. The 1.23B FineWeb comparison only includes RoPE, omitting ALiBi and modern long-context methods; vision experiments compare only against absolute positional embeddings, not stronger 2D relative/positional baselines. Several experiments also lack error bars or statistical significance tests.

Some claims are overstated. The assertion that standard attention is 'asymptotically unstable' depends on a low-signal/uniform-prior analysis, while trained standard attention can learn content sinks. The 'without computational overhead' claim is not fully demonstrated given projection and kernel details.

Reproducibility is only partially adequate: no code release is mentioned, and some figures report qualitative or incomplete numbers (e.g., DNA validation NLL and ImageNet in-distribution top-1 are not clearly tabulated), making exact replication harder.

Minor presentation issues remain, such as a missing plus sign in Eq. (20), inconsistent capitalization of Goat/GOAT, and dense small figures. Limitations are not explicitly discussed in a dedicated section.
